text:
Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. The argument for dropping it has an obvious appeal: children will spend their adult lives typing, so the hours spent looping letters together look like a nostalgic indulgence, a Victorian relic kept alive by sentiment and by teachers who learned it themselves. But the case against joined-up writing rests on a narrow picture of what handwriting is for, since it treats writing as a way of getting words onto a surface and measures a method by how quickly it gets there. Handwriting in the early years is doing a good deal more than that, and a fluent joined hand remains, for most children, the best way to do it.

Begin with the claim that keyboards have made handwriting obsolete. It is true that most adult text is now typed, but the school day is not the adult working day. Children write by hand constantly: in exercise books, on worksheets, in exams, on whiteboards, in the margins of a text they are trying to understand. In England and many other systems, high-stakes examinations are still written by hand, and will be for the foreseeable future, so a child who cannot write legibly and quickly under time pressure is disadvantaged in precisely the places where the stakes are highest. The relevant question is therefore not whether adults will handwrite, but whether a ten-year-old can produce a page of thoughtful prose in forty minutes without her hand cramping or her letters collapsing into illegibility. Fluent handwriting is a practical skill that bears directly on academic performance, and speed is a large part of it.

Joining matters here because printing, with each letter formed separately and the pen lifted between them, is slow: every lift and re-landing of the pen is a small decision. A joined hand reduces the number of pen lifts, builds rhythm, and lets the writer move across a word in a single flowing gesture, so that the letters of a word are learned as a sequence rather than as a pile of separate shapes. Researchers who study handwriting fluency have repeatedly found that automaticity, the point at which forming letters costs a child no conscious attention, is what frees working memory for composition. A child who is still thinking about how to make an "e" is not thinking about what she wants to say. Joined writing is one of the more reliable routes to that automaticity, because it turns a series of separate movements into a practised motor pattern, much as a pianist's scales turn single notes into phrases.

There is a fair objection, which is that some studies suggest the advantage of cursive over well-taught print is modest, and some adults who print quickly and neatly are perfectly effective writers. I do not claim that joined writing is the only road to fluency. I claim that it is the better default, and that the evidence for abandoning it is weaker than the enthusiasm of its critics suggests. Many of the most successful hands, in practice, are semi-joined: print-like letters with some natural links, developed from a cursive foundation. That is how most adults who write well actually write, having neither stayed with the stiff letter-by-letter print of the infant classroom nor adopted the formal copperplate of a historical copybook, but learned a joined system and then relaxed it into something personal and fast. Remove the joined foundation and you remove the route by which many children arrive at that mature, efficient hand.

The second reason concerns what handwriting does for the mind, which keyboards do not replicate. A growing body of work in cognitive science and neuroscience suggests that forming letters by hand engages the brain differently from pressing keys. Studies of young children learning letters have found that those who practise by writing them out recognise them more readily, and show more activation in reading-related brain regions, than those who type or trace them. The finger that presses "a" and the finger that presses "s" are doing the same kind of action; the hand that draws an "a" is making a shape that is distinct, effortful and uniquely the letter's own. That distinctness is a memory aid. Research on note-taking among older students points the same way, if less decisively: students who write notes by hand tend to process and summarise as they go, because they cannot keep up with a lecture word for word, and they often remember the material better. None of this is a conclusive argument for cursive specifically, and the literature is more mixed than headlines suggest. But it is an argument that the hand has a role in learning that a keyboard does not fill, and cursive, being the most practised and most continuous form of handwriting, makes the fullest use of that role.

Third, there is the matter of access to the written world. A child who cannot read cursive cannot read a great deal of it: a grandparent's birthday card, a handwritten recipe, a teacher's comment in a looped script, an archive of letters, the labels in a museum case, a historical document in a local record office. This sounds like a small thing until one imagines a generation that regards joined writing as an alien code. Literacy has always included the ability to read what other people have actually written, and what people write by hand is, to a large extent, joined. Teaching children to write cursive is the most efficient way to teach them to read it, since the two skills reinforce each other. Leaving reading of handwriting to chance would be an odd loss in a period when we are rightly anxious about children's access to their own cultural inheritance.

Fourth, and perhaps most persuasive to anyone who has worked in a classroom, joined writing helps with some of the specific difficulties that children face. For many pupils with dyslexia and related difficulties, the continuous movement of cursive reduces the reversals that plague print, since a "b" and a "d" begin and flow in clearly different directions, and the word is written as a unit. Children who struggle with spelling can sometimes benefit from the muscle memory of a written word pattern. Teachers of children with fine motor difficulties are often wary of relying on keyboards alone, because typing skills have to be taught as carefully as handwriting does, and a child who has been given a laptop in place of a pen has not necessarily been given a solution. It is a mistake to treat the keyboard as an automatic remedy for every difficulty with the hand.

That brings me to the best argument for the other side, which is time: the school day is crowded, the curriculum is overfull, and every hour of handwriting practice is an hour not spent on reading, mathematics, coding or touch typing. I take this seriously, and it is why I would not defend the long, joyless drills of earlier generations. But the real cost of teaching joined writing is small. A few short, well-structured sessions a week, in the early years, are enough to establish the habit, and the payoff comes back in every subsequent lesson where writing is required, which is nearly all of them. A child who writes fluently saves time everywhere else, and handwriting and typing are not in competition, since children should learn both, and the sensible position is that they should learn to write by hand first and to type properly later, once the hand has done its foundational work. The choice is not between the nineteenth century and the twenty-first. It is between giving children one skill and giving them two.

Finally, there is something to be said for the sheer ordinary value of a personal hand. A person's handwriting is one of the few things in the school curriculum that ends up being unmistakably their own: it is how they sign a document, write a card to a friend, leave a note on the fridge, and jot a thought they do not yet want to put on a screen. It carries a trace of the writer that no font can. That is not a reason to hold a child to a rigid model of how letters must look, and a good teacher will let a hand become individual, but it is a reason not to abandon the idea that a person should have one.

So the answer to whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting is yes, with the caveat that it should be taught sensibly: briefly, clearly, with a model that is simple and readable, and with the aim of fluency rather than ornament. The point is not to preserve a tradition for its own sake but to recognise that a fluent, joined hand gives children speed under pressure, a route to automaticity that frees their minds for ideas, a way of reading the written record around them, and a tool that supports those who find writing hardest. Remove it, and we lose those benefits for the sake of a saving in time that is far smaller than it appears. Keep it, and we give every child a useful, durable skill that costs little to teach and repays the effort for decades.
